exercise.title: Why is a thin shell approximately circumference times height times thickness?

statement.p: Cutting a thin cylindrical wall and flattening it produces a rectangle of width about 2\pi r. In your own words, why is that a good approximation, and why does the extra term involving (\Delta r)^2 disappear in the integral?

hint.p: Inner and outer circumferences differ, but the difference is higher-order small. The integral keeps the first-order piece and lets the error vanish in the limit.

subsection.title: When shells beat washers
subsection.p: The washer method uses slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. The shell method uses slices parallel to the axis of rotation.
That one choice can turn a difficult setup into a simple one.
A quick way to remember it is:

p.me: \text{slices perpendicular to the axis make disks or washers;}
\text{slices parallel to the axis make shells.}

exercise.title: Why do slices parallel to the axis make shells instead of washers?

statement.p: Disks and washers come from slices perpendicular to the axis of rotation. In your own words, why does a strip parallel to that axis sweep out a thin cylindrical wall, and how does that one choice of direction change the small piece?

hint.p: A strip perpendicular to the axis rotates in place and traces a disk or washer. A strip parallel to the axis is carried around the axis and traces a cylinder.

subsection.title: Comparing two methods on the same solid
subsection.p: Different methods should agree when they describe the same solid. The setup may look different, but the volume is the same physical quantity.

exercise.title: Why can shells and washers give the same volume?

statement.p: The two methods add different-looking pieces. In your own words, why is the method not the meaning, and why should two correct descriptions of the same solid agree?

hint.p: One adds thin cylindrical walls. The other adds thin cross-sectional washers. Both are ways of assembling the same three-dimensional object.

note.title: The method is not the meaning
note.p: Shells and washers are two ways to add the same solid. One adds thin cylindrical walls. The other adds thin cross-sectional washers. If both describe the same solid correctly, they give the same volume.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: A radius is a distance, so it is nonnegative. If a strip crosses the axis of rotation, or if symmetric strips produce the same shell, split the region or use symmetry.

subsection.p: Shells give one more way to choose the small piece. The next section changes the quantity being measured. Instead of adding volume, we add matter.
